name: Motorcycle
title: Twin-cylinder motorcycle (700 cc)
intro: This is a 700 cc parallel-twin motorcycle. Like a real one, the engine is sealed (the inside is bathed in oil). In a lesson the cases turn see-through so you can watch the pistons and crankshaft; explode it (🧩) to see the gearbox and chain. Ask me "Why do you need to change gear?"
suggest: How does the engine turn the wheel?
Why do you need to change gear?
Why is the front brake bigger?
looksLike: motorcycle, motorbike, bike, sport bike, scooter

ride.hint: You're in the rider's seat. Drag to look around; open the throttle and change gear to see how engine rpm and speed change; tap X-ray to see the engine and gearbox under your feet.

crankcase.name: Crankcase
crankcase.info: The aluminium case at the bottom of the engine. It holds the crankshaft, clutch and gearbox, all in oil, so nothing rusts and everything stays lubricated.

cylinder_block.name: Cylinder block
cylinder_block.info: Two cylinders side by side, tilted forward 15°. The pistons run up and down inside; a water jacket around them carries the heat away.

cylinder_head.name: Cylinder head
cylinder_head.info: Sits on top of the cylinders and holds the intake valves, exhaust valves and spark plugs. Combustion happens just below it.

cam_cover.name: Cam cover
cam_cover.info: The cover on the very top, over the two camshafts.

piston_r.name: Right piston
piston_r.info: Burning gas pushes it down, and through the connecting rod it turns the crankshaft. Right now it sits at the very top (top dead centre).

piston_l.name: Left piston
piston_l.info: The left cylinder's piston. It fires 270° after the right one, so the two pistons never move up and down together.

conrod_r.name: Right connecting rod
conrod_r.info: Links the piston to the crankshaft and turns the piston's up-and-down motion into the crankshaft's rotation.

crankshaft.name: Crankshaft
crankshaft.info: Its two crank throws are 270° apart. This "270° crank" makes a parallel twin sound and pull like a V-twin, with more rhythm.

primary_gear.name: Primary gear
primary_gear.info: A small gear (32 teeth) on the right end of the crankshaft. It drives the big gear (58 teeth) on the clutch basket, the first step down in speed.

camshaft_intake.name: Intake camshaft
camshaft_intake.info: Each cam lobe pushes an intake valve open as it comes round. It turns at half the crankshaft's speed.

camshaft_exhaust.name: Exhaust camshaft
camshaft_exhaust.info: Pushes the exhaust valves open, also at half the crankshaft's speed.

cam_chain.name: Cam chain
cam_chain.info: Drives the two camshafts up top from the crankshaft, so the valves always open in step with the pistons.

radiator.name: Radiator
radiator.info: The cooler in front of the engine. Coolant picks up heat from the cylinders, and the oncoming air cools it here.

exhaust_headers.name: Exhaust headers
exhaust_headers.info: Two pipes curving down from the front of the cylinder head, carrying the burnt gas back.

clutch.name: Clutch
clutch.info: A stack of friction plates. Squeeze the left lever and they part, disconnecting the engine from the gearbox so you can pull away and change gear.

clutch_cover.name: Clutch cover
clutch_cover.info: The round cover on the right side of the engine, over the clutch.

mainshaft.name: Mainshaft
mainshaft.info: The gearbox input shaft. It turns with the clutch and carries six gears.

countershaft.name: Countershaft
countershaft.info: The gearbox output shaft. Changing gear means a different pair of gears meshes: in 1st a small gear drives a big one for the most force; 6th is nearly one to one, the fastest.

sprocket_front.name: Front sprocket
sprocket_front.info: The small sprocket (15 teeth) on the end of the countershaft. It drives the chain.

chain.name: Drive chain
chain.info: Carries the force from the front sprocket to the big sprocket on the rear wheel.

sprocket_rear.name: Rear sprocket
sprocket_rear.info: The big sprocket (43 teeth) on the rear wheel. Small at the front, big at the back: another step down in speed and up in force.

frame.name: Frame
frame.info: The bike's skeleton. The engine, steering head and swingarm all hang from it.

fork.name: Front fork
fork.info: Two suspension tubes holding the front wheel. The whole fork turns about the steering axis, tilted 21°: that is how the bike steers.

handlebar.name: Handlebar
handlebar.info: Right hand: throttle and front brake. Left hand: clutch.

headlight_cowl.name: Headlight cowl
headlight_cowl.info: The front cover around the headlight and the instruments.

wheel_front.name: Front wheel
wheel_front.info: The front wheel is steered by the fork.

disc_front_l.name: Left front disc
disc_front_l.info: A steel disc that turns with the front wheel. When you brake, the caliper squeezes it and friction turns speed into heat.

disc_front_r.name: Right front disc
disc_front_r.info: The front wheel has two discs, because your weight shifts forward when braking and the front wheel does most of the braking.

calipers_front.name: Front calipers
calipers_front.info: Hydraulic pistons inside press the pads onto the discs when you pull the brake lever.

swingarm.name: Swingarm
swingarm.info: The rear wheel is mounted on it. Its front end pivots up and down, and the rear shock soaks up the bumps.

wheel_rear.name: Rear wheel
wheel_rear.info: The driven wheel, turned by the chain.

disc_rear.name: Rear disc
disc_rear.info: The rear brake disc, smaller than the front ones.

caliper_rear.name: Rear caliper
caliper_rear.info: Squeezes the rear disc when your right foot presses the brake pedal.

tank.name: Fuel tank
tank.info: Holds the petrol. The rider grips it with their knees.

seat.name: Seat
seat.info: Where the rider and passenger sit.

side_cover_l.name: Left side cover
side_cover_l.info: The side panel under the seat; the battery and the engine computer sit behind it.

tail.name: Tail
tail.info: The tail bodywork and the tail light.

steps.say: Burning gas pushes the piston down, and the connecting rod turns that up-and-down motion into the crankshaft's rotation.
The two crank throws are 270° apart, so the cylinders fire in turn and never move up and down together.

quiz.q: Why aren't the two pistons designed to move up and down together?
options: So the cylinders take turns, giving a smoother rhythm of power and sound
A 270° crank fires at uneven intervals, so it pulls and sounds like a V-twin; with the pistons out of step, some of the vibration cancels too.
To save material
It has nothing to do with material; it's about firing order and vibration.
Moving together would be better, it just can't be built
It can be built (a 360° crank); it simply vibrates and feels different.

steps.say: The cam chain drives the two camshafts up top, which open the intake and exhaust valves.

quiz.q: Why does the camshaft turn at only half the crankshaft's speed?
options: In a four-stroke engine each valve opens once every two crank turns
Intake, compression, power and exhaust take two turns of the crank, and each valve opens once, so one camshaft turn is exactly right.
To save fuel
The ratio comes from the four-stroke cycle.
It would break if it spun faster
The reason is the valve timing, not strength.

drive.title: From the engine to the rear wheel

steps.say: The small gear on the crankshaft drives the big gear on the clutch: the first step down in speed.
The clutch turns the gearbox mainshaft, whose gears mesh with the countershaft. Right now it's in 1st.
The small sprocket on the end of the countershaft pulls the chain, and the chain turns the big sprocket on the rear wheel.

quiz.q: Why is the rear sprocket so much bigger than the front one?
options: To reduce speed again, so the rear wheel turns slower but with more force
15 teeth driving 43 leaves the wheel turning at less than a third of the speed, so the push is nearly three times bigger: enough to get rider and bike moving.
It looks better
The size sets the gear ratio; it isn't styling.
To stop the chain falling off
Chain tension and tooth shape keep the chain on; the size is for reduction.

steps.say: 1st gear: a small gear on the mainshaft drives a big gear on the countershaft. The engine turns many times for each little turn of the rear wheel.
6th gear: the two gears are nearly the same size. At the same engine speed, the rear wheel turns almost three times faster.

quiz.q: Why do you pull away in 1st gear?
options: 1st gives the most force, enough to get moving from a stop
Getting going from standstill needs the biggest push, and 1st multiplies the engine's force the most. Once you're moving you shift up so the engine doesn't have to spin too fast.
1st gear saves fuel
High gears at low rpm save fuel.
6th stalls because its gears are too small
6th stalls because there isn't enough push and the engine is dragged down to too low an rpm.

steps.say: Before changing gear you pull the clutch, disconnecting the engine from the gearbox so the gears can slide across.
The whole fork turns about the tilted steering axis, and the front wheel steers with it.
The rear wheel is mounted on the swingarm. Over bumps the swingarm swings up and down, so the bike doesn't bounce.
The front wheel has two discs and two calipers; the rear has just one.

quiz.q: Why is the front brake bigger than the rear?
options: Weight shifts forward when braking, so the front tyre grips the most
When you slow down, the weight of bike and rider presses forward. The harder the front tyre is pressed, the better it grips, so it gets most of the braking force.
The front wheel is bigger
The wheels are about the same size; the reason is weight transfer when braking.
The rear wheel doesn't need a brake
The rear needs a brake too; it just gets a smaller share.

clutch_slip.title: Slipping clutch
clutch_slip.short: The engine revs in gear, but the bike won't go
clutch_slip.symptom: In 1st gear with the throttle open, the crankshaft spins fast, but the rear wheel barely moves. What do you think is broken?
clutch_slip.hint: Where does the engine's force go first, before it reaches the gearbox? Find the point after which everything stops.
clutch_slip.observe: The crankshaft spins fast. Find the first part that can't keep up.
whys: The chain is still on both sprockets. The problem is further forward: the mainshaft itself barely turns.
The engine spins fast, so it has power. The power is lost before it gets into the gearbox.
clutch_slip.cause: The clutch plates are worn and slipping. The clutch basket turns with the engine, but the gearbox mainshaft inside isn't driven.
clutch_slip.why: Why doesn't the rear wheel move with a slipping clutch, however fast the engine spins?
clutch_slip.answer: The clutch passes the engine's turning to the gearbox mainshaft through friction plates. When they slip past each other, the force never enters the gearbox, so the countershaft, chain and rear wheel get nothing.
reasons: A slipping clutch stalls the engine, so the rear wheel stops.
The clutch is the brake, and when it slips it holds the rear wheel.
